mainTopic: Finishing the health advice (bloodletting and כשות), then the משנה about a man who orders a גט and is then struck by קורדייקוס (temporary madness), and the מחלוקת between ריש לקיש and רבי יוחנן on when the גט is written.
overview: First the גמרא finishes two pieces of health advice: where blood is let from in an earlier remedy, and in which seasons eating כשות helps or harms. Then it returns to the משנה. A sane man orders a גט, is struck by קורדייקוס, and says 'don't write.' His retraction means nothing. ריש לקיש says the גט is written right away. רבי יוחנן says they wait until he is healed. ריש לקיש compares the man to a sleeper, and רבי יוחנן compares him to a שוטה, and the גמרא defends both comparisons. The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן from שמואל's ruling that a man whose throat was cut can order a גט by signs. It answers that that man's mind is clear, while the mad man's mind is confused. This leads to a discussion of whether such a man counts as alive and why the one who cut him is not exiled. Finally the גמרא turns to the mute husband in the משנה and asks how the court makes sure his nods are real answers. The ברייתא's test of asking about the seasons is still being worked out on the next amud.

steps.title: Defining 'below' and 'above' in the bloodletting remedy
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains where blood is let from in the remedy mentioned just before.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Below' means below the testicles. 'Above' means above the testicles.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an earlier medical remedy. It explains two words that were used there: 'below' and 'above'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier remedy said to let blood 'below' or 'above' but did not say below or above what. This line fills in that missing point of reference. Nothing new is argued here. It only makes the instruction clear.

phrases.english: 'Below' means below the testicles,
'Above' means above the testicles.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains words from the remedy discussed earlier on the דף.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In that remedy, 'below' and 'above' are measured from the testicles.

steps.title: Dodder is harmful out of season and good in season
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes 'כשות not in its time' from an earlier list of harmful things. Then it brings a teaching that כשות in its time is actually good.
steps.simpleTranslation: The list said: 'And כשות eaten not in its time' is harmful. A teaching adds: just as it is harmful when not in its time, it is good when in its time.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא picks up one item from an earlier list of harmful things, כשות eaten out of season. It brings a ברייתא that adds the other side: in season, כשות is healthy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The original list only gave the negative side. The תנא teaches that the season is what decides. The same plant can harm or help depending on when you eat it.

keyTerms.meaning: dodder, a plant that grows on other plants

phrases.english: And dodder not in its time.
It was taught: just as it is harmful not in its time,
so too it is good in its time.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next item in the health discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: כשות is harmful out of season and beneficial in season.

steps.title: רב פפא defines the seasons of dodder
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says which months are 'its time', which are 'not its time', and which are neutral.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Its time is תמוז. Not its time is טבת. In the days of ניסן and the days of תשרי it neither helps nor harms.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא explains what 'in its time' and 'not in its time' mean by giving actual months.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Summer (תמוז) is the good time and winter (טבת) is the harmful time. The in-between seasons, spring (ניסן) and autumn (תשרי), are neutral. So there are three categories, not just two.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: its time is Tammuz,
not in its time is Tevet,
the days of Nisan and the days of Tishrei —
they neither help nor harm.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the terms used in the ברייתא of step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תמוז is the beneficial season, טבת the harmful season, and ניסן and תשרי are neutral.
steps.whatToRemember: כשות: good in תמוז, harmful in טבת, neutral in ניסן and תשרי.

steps.title: The משנה: a man orders a גט, goes temporarily mad, and retracts
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה. A sane man orders a גט, is then struck by קורדייקוס, and says 'don't write.' His retraction counts for nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said, 'Write a גט for my wife,' and then קורדייקוס seized him, and he said, 'Don't write,' his last words mean nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה's הלכה. It quotes the case of a man who changes his mind while he is mentally unwell.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first order was given when he was sane, so it is valid. The retraction was said while he was mad, so it has no legal weight. This sets up the next question: does the בית דין act on his order right away, or wait?

phrases.english: If he said: 'Write a bill of divorce for my wife,'
phrases.notes: He said this while he was still thinking clearly.

phrases.english: and kordeyakos seized him,
and he then said: 'Do not write it' —
his last words are nothing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the medical discussion and returns to the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A retraction made during קורדייקוס does not cancel an order for a גט given while sane.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: write and give the גט right away
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש rules that the גט is written and given immediately, even while the husband is still mad.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן לקיש said: They write and give the גט immediately.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש gives his practical ruling on the משנה's case. They do not wait for the husband to recover.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the sane order still stands, ריש לקיש holds that it can be carried out now. The husband's current madness does not hold anything up.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said:
They write and give the bill of divorce immediately.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ: כּוֹתְבִין וְנוֹתְנִין גֵּט לְאַלְתַּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a ruling on how to carry out the משנה's case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The גט is written and given immediately, even during the madness.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: write only once he is healed
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן disagrees. The גט is written only after the husband recovers.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: They write it only once he is healed.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives the opposing view. The בית דין must wait until the husband is sane again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both agree that the retraction is worthless. They argue only about timing: right now, or after he recovers. The rest of this section looks at how each one reads the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: an אמורא, the main partner of ריש לקיש in debate

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יוחנן is NOT saying the retraction counts. He agrees the order stands. He only says the writing must wait until the husband recovers.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:
They write it only once he is healed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: אֵין כּוֹתְבִין אֶלָּא לִכְשֶׁיִּשְׁתַּפֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with ריש לקיש in step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The גט is written only after the husband recovers.

steps.title: What is ריש לקיש's reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what source supports ריש לקיש.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of ריש לקיש?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the basis of ריש לקיש's ruling. This sets up the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא wants to know what in the משנה led ריש לקיש to say the גט is written immediately.

keyTerms.meaning: short name for רבי שמעון בן לקיש

phrases.english: What is the reason of Reish Lakish?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source behind step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The textual basis for ריש לקיש's ruling to write the גט immediately.

steps.title: His reason: the משנה says the last words are nothing
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש learns from the משנה's words 'his last words are nothing' that the first order can be carried out now.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the משנה teaches: his last words are nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that ריש לקיש is reading the משנה's own words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the retraction is truly 'nothing', then only the sane order is left. Nothing stops the בית דין from acting on it right away.

phrases.english: Because it teaches: there is nothing in his last words.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה from step 4, with very slightly different wording.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה calls the retraction 'nothing', so the original order can be carried out right away.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן reads the same words differently
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that 'his last words are nothing' only means there is no need to ask him again after he recovers. The writing still waits until he is healed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן would tell you: 'There is nothing in his last words' means that when he becomes clear-minded, they do not need to go back and ask him again. But really, they write only once he is healed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רבי יוחנן can explain the same משנה words without agreeing with ריש לקיש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יוחנן, 'nothing' means the retraction does not force the בית דין to get a new order from the husband after he recovers. It does not mean they may write while he is mad. So the משנה is no proof for ריש לקיש.
steps.whatToRemember: Both agree the retraction during madness is worthless. ריש לקיש: write the גט immediately. רבי יוחנן: wait until he is healed, but there is no need to ask him again.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan would say to you:
'There is nothing in his last words' —
means that when he becomes clear-minded,
there is no need to go back and ask him again;
but really, they write it only once he is healed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns away the proof from the משנה in step 8 by reading it another way.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'His last words are nothing' seems to mean the גט may be written right away.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means only that no new order is needed after he recovers. The writing waits until he is healed.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the משנה as proof for ריש לקיש.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The words 'nothing in his last words' can be read as being about asking him again, not about when to write.

steps.title: What is the root of their argument?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what basic idea ריש לקיש and רבי יוחנן are arguing about.
steps.simpleTranslation: On what point do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the argument between ריש לקיש and רבי יוחנן. It is setting up the next line, which gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We already know what each one rules. Now the גמרא wants the logic underneath: how does each one view a man who is temporarily mad?

keyTerms.meaning: On what point do they disagree?

phrases.english: On what point do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the source-reading debate in steps 8-9, the גמרא asks for the core logic of the argument.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The underlying principle that splits ריש לקיש and רבי יוחנן.

steps.title: Sleeping person versus שוטה
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש compares the temporarily mad man to someone asleep. רבי יוחנן compares him to a שוטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש compares him to a sleeping person, and רבי יוחנן compares him to a שוטה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: each side compares the temporarily mad husband to a different kind of person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a man orders a גט and then falls asleep, we write it without waiting for him to wake up. So in ריש לקיש's view, the madness is only a pause. רבי יוחנן says that while the madness lasts, the man is like a שוטה, who cannot divorce, so we must wait.

keyTerms.meaning: a mentally incompetent person, who cannot give a גט

phrases.english: Reish Lakish compares him to a sleeping person,
phrases.notes: "Him" is the husband who gave the order and then was struck by the temporary madness.

phrases.english: and Rabbi Yochanan compares him to a shoteh.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ריש לקיש treats him like a sleeping person, whose order still stands. רבי יוחנן treats him like a שוטה, who cannot act right now.
steps.whyThisMatters: The whole argument now turns on one question: which comparison fits better? The next steps test both comparisons.

steps.title: Why doesn't רבי יוחנן also compare him to a sleeping person?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן: the sleeping-person comparison seems to fit, so why not use it?
steps.simpleTranslation: And let רבי יוחנן also compare him to a sleeping person!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes רבי יוחנן. Why not agree that this man is like someone asleep, whose order is carried out right away?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A sleeping person and a temporarily mad person are both out of action for a short while and then return to normal. So the comparison to sleep looks very natural, and רבי יוחנן must explain why he does not use it.

phrases.english: And let Rabbi Yochanan also compare him to a sleeping person!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests רבי יוחנן's side of the answer in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's choice to compare the man to a שוטה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Temporary madness looks like sleep, since both are short breaks from normal awareness. So why not follow the sleep comparison and write the גט now?

steps.title: A sleeper needs nothing done, but this man needs a cure
steps.stepSummary: A sleeping person wakes up by himself. The mad man needs an action, a remedy, to recover.
steps.simpleTranslation: A sleeping person is not lacking an action. This one is lacking an action.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רבי יוחנן. Sleep ends by itself, but this madness only ends if something is done to cure it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the sleeper's return to normal is automatic, he is treated as if he is still fully there. The mad man's recovery depends on an outside step, the remedy. So right now he is not like a sleeper, and רבי יוחנן treats him like a שוטה.

keyTerms.meaning: lacking an action; something still has to be done

phrases.english: A sleeping person is not lacking an action,
phrases.notes: He will wake up by himself; nobody has to do anything to him.

phrases.english: this one is lacking an action.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought temporary madness is just like sleep.
steps.terutzMaskana: Sleep ends on its own. This madness needs an action, a cure, so in רבי יוחנן's view the man is not like a sleeper.

steps.title: Why doesn't ריש לקיש also compare him to a שוטה?
steps.stepSummary: Now the גמרא challenges the other side: since the man is out of his mind right now, why doesn't ריש לקיש treat him like a שוטה?
steps.simpleTranslation: And let ריש לקיש also compare him to a שוטה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to ריש לקיש and asks why he does not agree that this man is like a שוטה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Right now the man really is not in his right mind, just like a שוטה. So ריש לקיש has to explain why that does not stop the גט from being written.

phrases.english: And let Reish Lakish also compare him to a shoteh!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending רבי יוחנן, the גמרא tests ריש לקיש's side in the same way.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's choice to compare the man to a sleeping person
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: While the madness lasts, the man is mentally unfit, like a שוטה. So why not wait, as one would for a שוטה?

steps.title: A שוטה has no cure, but this man has one in our hands
steps.stepSummary: There is no cure available for a שוטה. For this madness we do have a cure: red meat roasted on coals and well-diluted wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: A שוטה, his cure is not in our hands. This one, his cure is in our hands: red meat on coals, and diluted wine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for ריש לקיש. This man is different from a שוטה because we know how to cure him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the cure is easy and available, ריש לקיש sees the madness as a short, fixable condition, not like real שוטה status. So his earlier order can still be carried out now.

keyTerms.meaning: his cure is in our hands

phrases.english: A shoteh, his cure is not in our hands,
this one, his cure is in our hands:
red meat roasted on coals,
phrases.notes: This is the cure for this madness that the גמרא gave earlier (סז ע״ב).

phrases.english: and diluted wine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought anyone currently out of his mind is like a שוטה.
steps.terutzMaskana: A שוטה has no cure available. This man's cure is known and easy, so ריש לקיש does not treat him as a שוטה.
steps.whatToRemember: ריש לקיש: like a sleeper, since the cure is in our hands. רבי יוחנן: like a שוטה, since unlike a sleeper, he needs an action to recover.

steps.title: A challenge to רבי יוחנן from the man whose throat was cut
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא doubts that רבי יוחנן really holds we must wait. It brings שמואל's ruling: a man whose throat was cut who orders a גט by signs gets it written and given right away.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רבי יוחנן really say this? But רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: if someone's two pipes, or most of the two, were cut, and he signaled, saying "Write a גט for my wife", they should write it and give it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new challenge against רבי יוחנן's view that we must wait. It quotes שמואל's ruling as the start of the attack. Step 17 adds a ברייתא to strengthen it, and step 18 answers it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A man with his throat cut is in a very weak state and can only make signs, yet we write and give his גט at once without waiting. This seems to clash with רבי יוחנן's ruling that we wait for the mad man to recover.

keyTerms.meaning: his two pipes (windpipe and food pipe) were cut

steps.confusionAlert: This ruling is said by שמואל, not by רבי יוחנן. The גמרא is only using it to build a challenge against רבי יוחנן. Step 18 answers that challenge.

phrases.english: But did Rabbi Yochanan really say this?!
phrases.notes: "This" means his ruling that we must wait until the husband recovers.

phrases.english: But didn't Rav Yehuda say in the name of Shmuel:

phrases.aramaic: שָׁחַט בּוֹ שְׁנַיִם, אוֹ רוֹב שְׁנַיִם,
phrases.english: if someone cut his two pipes, or most of the two pipes,
phrases.notes: The two pipes are the windpipe and the food pipe in the throat.

phrases.english: and he signaled and said: "Write a get for my wife" –
then these people should write it and give it;

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הָכִי וְהָאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After both comparisons are defended, the גמרא opens a new attack on רבי יוחנן's position from an outside source.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that the גט waits until the husband recovers
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In שמואל's ruling, a man in a desperate, failing state who orders a גט only by signs has it written and given right away. That seems hard to square with requiring a wait in the madness case. Step 17 strengthens this challenge with a ברייתא.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports שמואל: even a crucified man can order a גט
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that if a man with severed limbs or a crucified man signals 'write a גט for my wife', it is written and given. This strengthens the challenge against רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a ברייתא teaches: If people saw a man with his limbs cut off, or hanging on a cross, and he signaled and said, 'Write a גט for my wife,' they should write it and give it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that agrees with שמואל's ruling from the last step. This adds weight to the question on רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This man is certainly dying and can only communicate by signs, yet we write the גט immediately and do not wait. So why does רבי יוחנן say we must wait for the mad man to recover? The ברייתא makes the challenge from step 16 stronger.

keyTerms.meaning: And it was taught (in a ברייתא), introducing a supporting source
A person whose limbs have been cut off
He signaled, gave a sign or hint

phrases.english: And it was taught: if they saw him with limbs cut off
or crucified on the cross,
and he signaled and said:
'Write a bill of divorce for my wife'
then these people should write and give it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a ברייתא that supports שמואל's ruling, strengthening the challenge to רבי יוחנן.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that a גט is written right away even for a dying man who communicates only by signs, against רבי יוחנן's requirement to wait.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a man with severed limbs or a crucified man.

steps.title: A dying man's mind is clear, but the mad man's mind is confused
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the comparison. The dying man thinks clearly and is only physically weak; the mad man's mind itself is confused.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can you compare them? There, his mind is clear, and only weakness has started to set into his body. Here, his mind is confused.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי יוחנן by showing that the two cases are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גט needs a husband who understands what he is doing. The crucified man's body is failing, but his thinking is fine, so his signals count. The mad man's thinking itself is broken, so we must wait until he is cured.

keyTerms.meaning: How can you compare? (rejecting a comparison)

steps.whatToRemember: What counts for a גט is a clear mind, not a strong body. A dying man with a clear mind can order a גט; a confused mind cannot.

phrases.english: How can you compare?!
There, his mind is clear,
and it is only weakness that has begun in him;
here, his mind is confused.
phrases.notes: 'Here' is the man struck by the temporary madness that רבי יוחנן was talking about.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from שמואל and the ברייתא by showing the cases are different.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (mental clarity versus physical weakness)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since we write a גט right away for a dying man who can only signal, we should do the same for the mad man.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dying man's mind is clear and only his body is weak; the mad man's mind is confused, so רבי יוחנן still requires waiting.

steps.title: Does שמואל really treat a man with a cut throat as alive?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions שמואל's ruling, because elsewhere שמואל says witnesses may testify that a man whose throat was cut is dead, even if he ran off.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did שמואל really say this? But רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: If someone cut both pipes in his throat, or most of both, and he ran away, witnesses may testify about him. If you think he is alive, why may they testify about him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to a new question: it points out what looks like a contradiction between two rulings of שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the גט ruling, שמואל treats the man with a cut throat as alive, since a dead man cannot give a גט. But in his other ruling, witnesses can say he is dead so his wife may remarry, even though nobody saw him die. Both cannot seem true.

keyTerms.meaning: But did he really say? (introducing a contradiction)
Both throat pipes, or most of both
Witnesses may testify about him (that he died)

phrases.english: But did Shmuel really say this?!
But didn't Rav Yehuda say in the name of Shmuel:

phrases.aramaic: שָׁחַט בּוֹ שְׁנַיִם אוֹ רוֹב שְׁנַיִם,
phrases.english: If he cut both pipes in him, or most of both,
phrases.notes: The two pipes are the windpipe and the food pipe in the throat.

phrases.english: and he ran away, they may testify about him.
phrases.notes: They testify that he is dead, so his wife may remarry.

phrases.english: And if you think he is alive,
why may they testify about him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the רבי יוחנן discussion and asks whether שמואל's own ruling from step 16 contradicts another ruling of his.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that a man whose throat was cut can order a גט
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Contradiction: שמואל lets witnesses testify that such a man is dead, which seems to mean he is treated as already dead, so how can he give a גט?

steps.title: He is alive now, but he will certainly die
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא resolves the contradiction: the man is alive right now, so he can give a גט, but he is sure to die soon, so witnesses can testify about his death.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answer: He is alive, but in the end he will die.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction in שמואל's rulings with one short line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both rulings are about the same man at different times. Right now he is alive and can order a גט. Since a cut like that always kills, witnesses can be sure he died later, even though they did not see it.

keyTerms.meaning: And in the end he will die

steps.whatToRemember: A man with a cut throat is alive for now, so he can order a גט, and he is certain to die, so witnesses may testify that he died.

phrases.english: They say: he is alive,
but in the end he will die.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reconciling both rulings by separating present status from certain future outcome
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Allowing testimony that he died means שמואל treats him as already dead.
steps.terutzMaskana: He is legally alive now, so he can give a גט, and his death is certain, so testimony about his death is allowed.

steps.title: If he is sure to die, why isn't the killer exiled?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: if a man with a cut throat is sure to die, the one who cut him should go to גלות. But a ברייתא says he does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if that is so, the one who cut him should be exiled because of him! Why then does a ברייתא teach: If he cut the two pipes in his throat, or most of the two, he is not exiled?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the idea from step 20 that a man with a cut throat is sure to die. It points to a ברייתא that says the person who accidentally cut him is not sent to גלות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who kills by accident goes to גלות, a city of refuge. If cutting the throat makes death certain, the person who did the cutting is the killer and should be exiled. The ברייתא says he is not exiled, so it looks like the victim is not treated as dead.

keyTerms.meaning: But if that is so: a way of pushing an idea to a result that seems wrong
Is exiled to a city of refuge for killing by accident
Both throat pipes (windpipe and food pipe), or most of both
Why then does a ברייתא teach

phrases.english: But if that is so,
the one who cut him should be exiled on his account!
Why then is it taught:

phrases.aramaic: שָׁחַט בּוֹ שְׁנַיִם אוֹ רוֹב שְׁנַיִם –
phrases.english: If he cut the two pipes in him, or most of the two,
he is not exiled?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה, יְהֵא גּוֹלֶה עַל יָדוֹ! אַלְּמָה תַּנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 20 that a man with a cut throat is sure to die.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a man whose throat was cut is treated as certain to die
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If death is certain, the person who cut him is the killer and should go to גלות, but a ברייתא says he does not.

steps.title: Other causes may have helped bring his death
steps.stepSummary: רבי הושעיא explains that maybe the wind, or the victim's own thrashing, added to his death. So the person who cut him is not the only killer and is not exiled.
steps.simpleTranslation: Wasn't it already said about this ברייתא: רבי הושעיא said, We worry that maybe the wind confused him and weakened him. Or also, maybe he himself sped up his own death.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא was already explained by רבי הושעיא. The killer is not exiled because something else may have helped cause the death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The victim really is sure to die, so step 20 still holds. But גלות is only for someone who is fully the killer. If the wind or the victim's own thrashing may have helped, the cutter is not exiled. Two possible extra causes are given.

keyTerms.meaning: Wasn't it already said about it: pointing to an explanation already given
We worry; we take the possibility into account
The wind confused him and weakened him
He sped up his own death

phrases.english: Wasn't it said about it,
Rabbi Hoshaya said:
We worry that perhaps the wind confused him.
phrases.notes: The idea is that air hitting the open wound may have helped kill him, so the cutter didn't do it alone.

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי, הוּא קֵירַב אֶת מִיתָתוֹ.
phrases.english: Or also, he himself brought his death closer.
phrases.notes: "He" is the victim, who sped up his death by thrashing around.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא אִיתְּמַר עֲלַהּ, אָמַר רַבִּי הוֹשַׁעְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains that the ruling of no גלות rests on a separate reason, not on the victim being alive
steps.terutzHavaAmina: No גלות means the victim is not treated as dead
steps.terutzMaskana: He is sure to die, but the cutter is not exiled because other causes may have helped bring the death
steps.whatToRemember: A man whose throat was cut is sure to die. The cutter is still not exiled, because the wind or the victim's own thrashing may have helped kill him.

steps.title: What difference is there between the two reasons?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference there is between the wind reason and the thrashing reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question to set up the next step. When would the two explanations of רבי הושעיא give different results?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both reasons lead to the same ruling in the ברייתא: no גלות. The גמרא wants a case where only one reason applies, so the two explanations would split.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between them?

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the two reasons given in step 22.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A case where the wind reason and the thrashing reason give different results

steps.title: Marble house with thrashing, or open field without thrashing
steps.stepSummary: Inside a marble house, there is no wind but the victim thrashed. In an open field, there is wind but he did not thrash. In each case only one reason applies.
steps.simpleTranslation: The difference is when he cut him in a marble house and the victim thrashed. Or also, when he cut him in an open field and the victim did not thrash.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question with two cases. In each case only one of the two reasons fits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a closed marble house, wind cannot be blamed, but thrashing can. So by the wind reason the cutter is exiled, and by the thrashing reason he is not. In an open field with no thrashing, it is the other way around.

keyTerms.meaning: A marble house: a closed room with no wind
Thrashed or twitched in the death struggle

phrases.english: There is a difference between them
where he cut him in a marble house, and he thrashed.
phrases.notes: A closed marble room has no wind, so only the thrashing reason could apply.

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי, דְּשַׁחְטֵיהּ בְּבָרָא, וְלָא פַּירְכֵּס.
phrases.english: Or also, where he cut him outside, and he did not thrash.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Marble house with thrashing: exiled by the wind reason, not by the thrashing reason. Open field without thrashing: the opposite.

steps.title: Maybe the mute man's nods are a shaking he cannot control
steps.stepSummary: Going back to the משנה about a mute man who answers by signals, the גמרא asks: maybe he has a shaking of 'no, no' or 'yes, yes' that he cannot control.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: If he became mute, and they said to him, 'Shall we write a גט for your wife?' and so on. But we should worry that maybe a shaking of 'no, no' took hold of him, or maybe a shaking of 'yes, yes' took hold of him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to quote the משנה about a man who became mute and answers by nodding. Then it challenges how we can trust his nods.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lets the court accept his head signals as real answers. The גמרא worries his head might be moving on its own, side to side ('no') or up and down ('yes'), with no real meaning behind it. If so, his signals would prove nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Became mute; lost the power to speak
A shaking or twitching movement he cannot control

phrases.english: If he became mute, and they said to him:
'Shall we write a bill of divorce for your wife?' and so on.
But let us worry that perhaps
a shaking of 'no, no' took hold of him,

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי שִׁיחְיָא דְּ״הֵן הֵן״ נַקְטֵיהּ!
phrases.english: or also, a shaking of 'yes, yes' took hold of him!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֵיחוּשׁ דִּלְמָא שִׁיחְיָא דְּ״לָאו לָאו״ נַקְטֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion about the man with a cut throat and returns to the next line of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that a mute man's nods are accepted for writing a גט
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: His head may be moving on its own, so his 'yes' or 'no' signals may not show what he really wants.

steps.title: The court asks alternating questions
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers the worry about shaking. The court asks questions that switch between needing a 'yes' and needing a 'no.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף בר מניומי said in the name of רב נחמן: we ask him questions in an alternating way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 25. A shaking he cannot control would not match questions whose answers keep switching between 'yes' and 'no.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: An uncontrolled shake would make the same motion every time, all 'yes' or all 'no.' If the court asks one question that needs 'no' and then one that needs 'yes,' and he answers each one correctly, his answers must be on purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: in an alternating way, switching back and forth
the אמורא whose answer is reported here

phrases.english: Rav Yosef bar Minyumi said
that Rav Naḥman said:
that we say to him alternating questions.
phrases.notes: Some questions need a 'yes' answer and some need a 'no' answer, mixed together.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 25 about a shaking he cannot control.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines how the court checks him so that his answers can be trusted
steps.terutzHavaAmina: His nods could be a shaking of 'yes, yes' or 'no, no' that he cannot control.
steps.terutzMaskana: Questions with switching answers rule out a steady shake.

steps.title: Maybe the shaking itself switches back and forth
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: what if his shaking also switches between 'yes' and 'no'?
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us worry that maybe a switching shake has taken hold of him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן's answer. Maybe the man has a shake that goes 'yes, no, yes, no' on its own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Alternating questions only work if a shake always makes the same motion. If the shake also alternates, it could happen to match the questions exactly. Then the test proves nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: a shaking or bending of the head that he cannot control

phrases.english: But let us be concerned that perhaps
an alternating shaking has taken hold of him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the test given in Step 26.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A shake that itself alternates could line up with alternating questions, so the test cannot tell a real answer from a shake.

steps.title: Use an uneven pattern of answers
steps.stepSummary: The court asks questions in an uneven pattern: one 'no' then two 'yes,' then two 'no' then one 'yes.'
steps.simpleTranslation: We ask him questions where the answers go: one 'no' and two 'yes,' and two 'no' and one 'yes.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The pattern of answers is made uneven, so even a switching shake could not match it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A shake that switches back and forth follows a simple, steady rhythm. An uneven order like no-yes-yes-no-no-yes breaks any steady rhythm. If he still answers each question correctly, he must understand.
steps.whatToRemember: The court rules out every kind of shake he cannot control by using an uneven pattern of 'yes' and 'no' questions.

phrases.english: That we say to him once 'no' and twice 'yes,'
phrases.notes: These are the answers the questions call for, not words the court says to him.

phrases.english: and twice 'no' and once 'yes.'

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמְרִינַן לֵיהּ חַד לָאו וּתְרֵין הֵן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 27 by making the test sharper.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A switching shake could match alternating questions.
steps.terutzMaskana: An uneven pattern cannot be matched by any steady shake.

steps.title: Another test: summer questions in winter
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא from the school of רבי ישמעאל gives a different test. The court asks him about summer things in the rainy season, and about rainy-season things in summer.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ישמעאל taught: we say to him things of the summer days during the rainy days, and things of the rainy days during the summer days.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching with another way to test whether the man understands. It asks about things that do not fit the season.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he understands, he will say 'no' to things that do not fit the season. This checks that his mind is clear, not only that his nods are on purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: the school of רבי ישמעאל taught (a ברייתא)

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:

phrases.aramaic: אוֹמְרִים לוֹ דְּבָרִים שֶׁל יְמוֹת הַחַמָּה
phrases.english: We say to him matters of the summer
during the rainy season,
and matters of the rainy season during the summer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, separate way to test the man's understanding.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The court tests him with questions about things that do not fit the season.

steps.title: What are these season questions?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what exactly these summer and winter questions are.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are they?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the details of the ברייתא's test. This sets up the next step, where a first guess is offered and rejected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא did not say which questions to ask. The גמרא needs an example that truly shows whether he understands.

phrases.english: What are they?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the details of the ברייתא in Step 29.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which seasonal matters the court asks about.

steps.title: Coats and sheets do not prove anything
steps.stepSummary: A first guess is that they ask about a warm coat or a thin sheet. The גמרא rejects it, because a sick person might really need a coat in summer or a sheet in winter.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say coats and sheets, let us worry that maybe a chill has taken hold of him, or that heat has taken hold of him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the example of a warm coat and a thin sheet, then attacks it. A 'yes' answer could make sense if he is sick.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test only works if a correct-thinking person would surely say 'no.' A man with chills might really want a coat in summer. A man with a fever might really want a thin sheet in the rainy season. So a 'yes' does not show that his mind is confused.

keyTerms.meaning: if you say (a guess the גמרא will reject)

phrases.english: If you say coats and sheets –
phrases.notes: A coat is for winter and a sheet is for summer; he is asked about each one in the wrong season.

phrases.english: let us worry that perhaps chills have taken hold of him,
or else heat has taken hold of him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a possible answer to the question of Step 30 and attacks it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The guess that the seasonal questions are about coats and sheets
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Because of chills or fever, a sick man could truly want these out of season, so a 'yes' does not show confusion.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only this example of the ברייתא's test, not the test itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The answer could be correct for a sick man, so it does not test his understanding.
